object_description: isolated, well-proportioned cuboid solitaire with much of the programme in the basement
geometry_property: transverse atrium with two spiral staircases
design_condition: a single cuboid mediates neutrally between the three surrounding urban structures, relocating a substantial part of the programme underground so the volume stays well scaled and distant from its built environment

positive: The stand-alone building neutrally mediates between the three surrounding urban structures
The extensive programme is combined in a single cuboid introducing a new, fourth urbanistic element
It is economically and energetically efficient
The building is well proportioned, appears extremely scaled and keeps sufficient distance from its environment
Relocating a substantial part of the programme to the basement makes this possible
Large atriums and extra-high room configurations bring natural side light to the buried teaching rooms
The open space concept creates well-usable areas with low sealing and high biodiversity
Rainwater management is well thought out and green roofs and photovoltaics are in balance
The garden facing the hillside forms a harmonious transition to the villa gardens
The building is amazingly clear and effectively organised inside
The huge but not oversized transverse atrium is airy, spectacular and extremely meaningful
It links teaching, research and all departments visually, functionally and symbolically
Programme, communication and orientation are therefore almost ideal
The heavily elevated glazed ground floor reads as a continuation of the public forecourt
The modular facades above are simple and elegant, restrained and timeless
The enlarged volume fulfils the required spatial programme without much loss of scale
The ground floor and lower basement reorganisation allowed the second basement to be much reduced
The spatial sequence of forecourt, foyer and atrium is as smooth as it is impressive
The attractiveness of the restaurant and student bar is improved
The arrangement of the two open spiral staircases has been sensitively revised
The deeper northern wing enables direct spatial connection between teaching rooms and institutes
Construction costs are within the specifications
negative: The student bar does not seem very inviting and some teaching rooms receive no natural light
The usage density appears to be too high
The open spaces are generously dimensioned but only moderately clearly formulated
The space towards the historic centre is spatially undecided
Its mineral surface is affected by the round atrium perforations and a conspicuous water channel
The garden also suffers from the light holes
The underpass exit appears taken over by the building and is unnecessarily cramped
Delivery and bicycle parking are unsatisfactory
The wide staircase cut into the ground floor leads surprisingly and irritatingly backwards and down
The coolness radiating from the atrium could be toned down with more welcoming materials
High noise levels are expected in the atrium, making the open areas problematic
Daylight to the teaching rooms via their narrow side is unfavourable
Whether such a sober industrial appearance suits a traditional university is questioned
The enlarged volume reduces and largely underdevelops the open space
The rectangular atrium cuts fragment the open spaces
The urban square still offers little quality of stay and the western garden acts as a residual area
The fitness area is awkwardly divided into two unconnected zones
The interior design remains sketchy and somewhat conventional
Noise development from the foyer is considered problematic
Flexibility is severely limited by extremely restrictive fire protection conditions
The redesigned facade evokes associations with an office building rather than the institution
The large glass sheds lack delicacy and the high glazing is energetically unfavourable and hard to clean
The energy concept and building technology are classified as unsustainable and life cycle costs are above target
